clue.text: Gas let off by a politician

blocks.note: a gun that is let off has been fired
taken as written
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician breaking wind in the chamber, the old joke about hot air.
explanation.walkthrough: Firedamp is the explosive methane found in coal mines; 'let off' reads as releasing wind but here means discharged.
explanation.definitionFit: Firedamp is the miners' name for methane, a flammable gas that collects underground.

clue.text: Celebrity in stage musical

blocks.note: first meaning: renown, being widely known
second meaning: the 1980s musical about a New York performing arts school

explanation.surface: A celebrity starring in a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity as an abstract noun means fame, and Fame is the title of a well-known musical.

clue.text: Hacienda owner sprinted and caught the woman

blocks.note: sprinted is ran fast
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a pronoun for the woman

explanation.surface: A ranch owner chasing down and catching a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacienda is a large ranch or estate in Spanish-speaking countries, run by a rancher.

clue.text: Criminal element mostly after speed abroad

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
abroad suggests wandering far afield, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: taken as written
radon, the radioactive gas, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A criminal element fleeing abroad at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal element' reads as a phrase, but the definition is the first word and 'element' is a chemical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw, a criminal of the Wild West kind.

clue.text: Dog fends tribesman off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the two words supply all fourteen letters

explanation.surface: A dog guarding its master by keeping a tribesman at bay.
explanation.definitionFit: Man's best friend is the proverbial name for the dog, prized for loyalty.

clue.text: A plank on a yacht maybe

blocks.note: taken as written
a plank is a length of board

explanation.surface: A sailor's plank lying on the deck of a yacht.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone aboard is on a vessel; a yacht is one example, hence 'maybe'.

clue.text: Screen idol, at the end, crashing bore

indicators.note: at the end points to the final letter of the word just named
crashing into something means breaking in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a bind is a tedious nuisance, a bore
the final letter of idol

explanation.surface: A screen idol crashing into a tedious person at the end of a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screen idol' runs together as a film star, but 'Screen' alone is the definition. A bind is British slang for something tiresome.
explanation.definitionFit: A blind is a window covering that screens out light or view.

clue.text: A row about the Spanish studio

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece is wrapped around the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a tier is a row of seats
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: An argument breaking out over the Spanish studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' suggests an argument but is a tier of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: An atelier is an artist's or designer's workshop, a studio.

clue.text: Send in lady to reform theme park

indicators.note: to reform is to reshape, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the three words supply all ten letters

explanation.surface: Packing a wayward woman off to be straightened out at an amusement park.
explanation.definitionFit: Disneyland in California is the original Disney theme park, opened in 1955.

clue.text: Son was sent up by barrister, one provoking debate

indicators.note: in a down clue, sent up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
to have lived is to have been, so was
an advocate pleads in court, as a barrister does

explanation.surface: A son mocked by a barrister who likes stirring up arguments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent up' looks like mockery but reverses the son and the verb together.
explanation.definitionFit: A devil's advocate argues the opposing side deliberately to provoke discussion.

clue.text: Month in America below zero

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for month
taken as written
US is the United States of America

explanation.surface: A winter month in the US when the temperature falls below freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like an instruction to insert, but it simply supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A minus temperature is one under zero, so the word stands for 'below zero' as an adjective.

clue.text: Poverty's end is seen in reform

indicators.note: something in reform is being reshaped, so the preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: the three words supply all nine letters

explanation.surface: A reforming politician promising that poverty is finally coming to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poverty's' reads as possessive, but it is 'Poverty is', joining the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Neediness is the state of being in want, a close synonym for poverty.

clue.text: Excite them with incredible nursery rhyme

indicators.note: to excite is to stir up, so the letters that follow are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A storyteller thrilling children with an amazing nursery rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two words of fodder rather than separating definition from wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Three Blind Mice is a well-known English nursery rhyme about mice chased by a farmer's wife.

clue.text: Miserable girl in police van

blocks.note: a black mood is a miserable one
a girl's name

explanation.surface: An unhappy girl sitting in a police van after arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Maria is the old slang name for a police van used to carry prisoners.

clue.text: Tar at sea with sail and ropes

indicators.note: at sea means confused and all over the place, so the letters are muddled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor (a tar) at sea handling sails and ropes.
explanation.walkthrough: Tar is old slang for a sailor, which makes 'at sea' look literal; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lariats are lassos, long ropes with a running noose used by cowboys.

clue.text: Quite a few cut off by a lake

blocks.note: to sever is to cut off
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Many people stranded by a lake, cut off from the outside world.
explanation.definitionFit: Several means more than two but not many, an everyday equivalent of 'quite a few'.

clue.text: Be unsteady, unwell during leave

indicators.note: during places one thing within the span of another, so it goes inside

blocks.note: to vacate a place is to leave it
ill means unwell

explanation.surface: Someone wobbly on their feet, having fallen sick while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' tempts as a noun, a holiday, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To vacillate is to waver, swaying between choices or physically, as if unsteady.

clue.text: Order to desist, so visit cancelled

blocks.note: to call on someone is to visit
an event that is off has been cancelled

explanation.surface: Someone told to stop, so the planned visit is cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay half also hints at the answer's everyday sense, since calling something off cancels it.
explanation.definitionFit: To call off, as with dogs or an attack, is to order them to stop.

clue.text: Odd having passionate desire over a period of five years

blocks.note: lust is passionate desire
rum is British slang for odd or peculiar

explanation.surface: A strange tale of someone burning with desire for five whole years.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts the desire on top of the odd word.
explanation.definitionFit: A lustrum is a five-year span, from the Roman purification ceremony held every five years.

clue.text: Choice of words found in short stories beginning differently

indicators.note: a word beginning differently keeps all but its first letter, which is swapped for another

blocks.note: short stories are works of fiction

explanation.surface: A writer's choice of words in short stories, with each beginning in a different way.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening F is swapped for a D; the clue leaves the new letter for the solver to find from the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Diction is a writer's or speaker's selection and style of vocabulary.

clue.text: Soldier taken over impressive base

indicators.note: taken over means turned upside down, so in a down clue the letters run upward

blocks.note: GI is an American soldier
noble means grand and impressive

explanation.surface: A soldier seized at an impressive military base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'base' looks like a military camp but is the adjective meaning low.
explanation.definitionFit: Base and ignoble both mean morally low or dishonourable.

clue.text: Fictional lawyer and policeman row pointing to boundary

blocks.note: Perry Mason is the defence lawyer of Erle Stanley Gardner's novels and the TV series
PC George Dixon of the old BBC series Dixon of Dock Green, a classic British bobby
a row is a line

explanation.surface: A lawyer from fiction and a police officer having an argument about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' tempts as an argument but means a line. Dixon of Dock Green was a long-running British TV police drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mason-Dixon line is the historic boundary between Pennsylvania and Maryland, dividing North from South.

clue.text: Well-known record, Donovan's first

indicators.note: first picks out just the opening letter of the name before it

blocks.note: to note something is to record it
the opening letter of Donovan

explanation.surface: The 1960s singer Donovan's famous debut record.
explanation.walkthrough: Donovan was a Scottish folk singer, which makes 'record' look like a disc.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means famous or distinguished, the same as well-known.

clue.text: Guide boy round centre of Amsterdam

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter
round means encircling, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
the fifth of nine letters

explanation.surface: Showing a boy around central Amsterdam.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead someone is to guide them, going ahead to show the way.

clue.text: Playing air twice (short tune), 'Land of Hope . . .'

indicators.note: short means the word lacks its final letter
playing something like music reworks it, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word air written out twice
the word tune without its last letter

explanation.surface: A band twice playing a short tune, the patriotic 'Land of Hope and Glory'.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on Elgar's 'Land of Hope and Glory': Ruritania is the land invented by the novelist Anthony Hope.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the fictional kingdom of Anthony Hope's novel The Prisoner of Zenda, so it is Hope's land.

clue.text: Stroll back, then head off

indicators.note: with its head off, a word loses its first letter

blocks.note: to back a horse is to gamble on it

explanation.surface: Walk back, then set off home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' looks like a direction for walking or a reversal signal, but it is a verb meaning to bet.
explanation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a leisurely pace, the same as a stroll.

clue.text: Notice, on inlet, a large number of ships

indicators.note: in an across clue, placing one thing on another means it comes after it

blocks.note: an arm of the sea is an inlet
AD is short for advertisement, a notice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sighting: many ships gathered in an inlet.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means after, so the notice follows the inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: An armada is a fleet of warships, most famously the Spanish one of 1588.

clue.text: Clergyman never terribly overdrawn?

indicators.note: terribly means badly done, so the letters come out disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
an overdrawn account is in the red

explanation.surface: A vicar who is never overdrawn, asked with mock surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram covers both the written word and the colour for being overdrawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverend is a member of the clergy, from the title 'the Reverend'.
